articles.title: Morphological analysis of the eye of Eudocimus ruber (Linnaeus, 1758).
articles.authors: Iara Fernanda Lima do Espírito Santo, Érika Branco, Elane Guerreiro Giese et al.
articles.abstract: Eudocimus ruber (Linnaeus, 1758), commonly known as the scarlet ibis, is a wading bird widely distributed throughout northern South America and along the Brazilian coast. However, detailed information on the ocular morphology of this species remains limited. Therefore, this study aimed to perform a multimodal morphological characterization of the eye and its associated structures in E. ruber. Eight specimens were used, and the heads were subjected to radiographic and computed tomographic examinations, followed by gross anatomical dissection, three-dimensional reconstruction, histological processing, and scanning electron microscopy. Gross anatomy revealed laterally positioned, flat-shaped eyes, eight extraocular muscles, a well-developed Harderian gland, and a pleated pecten oculi. Radiographic, tomographic, and three-dimensional analyses enabled visualization of the scleral ring and its anatomical position within the orbit. Histological examination identified the fibrous, vascular, and retinal tunics, including the scleral ossicles, scleral cartilage, ciliary body, iris, 10-layered retina, annular pad, pleated pecten oculi, Harderian gland, eyelids, and third eyelid. The scleral ossicles followed the type A overlap pattern according to the Lemmrich convention. The ocular morphology of E. ruber was generally consistent with that described in other avian species, with interspecific variation observed in several anatomical features. These findings expand the available anatomical knowledge of Threskiornithidae and provide a basis for future comparative studies of avian ocular morphology.

articles.title: Bench-stepping training improves stair-walking dynamics in older women: Evidence from an exploratory nonlinear kinematic analysis.
articles.authors: Remco J Baggen, Kimberley S van Schooten, Evelien Van Roie et al.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Stair walking challenges balance and coordination in older people. Bench-stepping training improves stair climbing speed in healthy older women. This study assessed whether bench-stepping also improves dynamic balance and movement complexity during stair walking. METHODS: Secondary analyses of stair walking data from a previous study involving 45 healthy older women (69 y ± 4) that assessed the effects of a 12-week bench-stepping intervention. Centre-of-mass acceleration was measured during stair ascent and descent. Linear dynamics included time, acceleration magnitude, and harmonic ratios (HR; indicating symmetry). Movement complexity was quantified using nonlinear dynamics including sample entropy (SampEn), recurrence quantification analysis (RQA), and fractal dimension (FD). RESULTS: For stair ascent, increased speed (p = 0.018, R²partial =0.093,) was accompanied by proportional increases in acceleration magnitudes (p ≤ 0.039, R²partial = 0.078-0.101). SampEn decreased more in the intervention group (p ≤ 0.012, R²partial = 0.049-0.101), indicating more predictable dynamics. In contrast, for stair descent, no changes in speed or acceleration magnitudes were observed. However, SampEn (p = 0.001, R²partial =0.082) and maximum RQA line length (p = 0.008, R²partial =0.057) of vertical acceleration increased significantly compared to controls, indicating lower predictability and more persistent recurring patterns. No significant changes were found for other outcomes. Exploratory factor analysis revealed distinct differences in motor behaviour between stair ascent and descent. CONCLUSION: Bench-stepping training induced measurable changes in stair walking dynamics. Specifically, sample entropy shows potential as a sensitive marker of altered motor complexity, particularly of vertical accelerations. Interestingly, the direction of changes in unpredictability differed between stair ascent and descent, suggesting different underlying control strategies.

articles.title: Cortical hemodynamic correlates of postural sway frequency redistribution during sensory-challenged quiet standing.
articles.authors: Di Yang, Baiyang Qiu, Yinuo Shuai et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Standing balance requires continual adjustment to the available sensory information. How changes in sway frequency composition relate to cortical hemodynamic responses during quiet standing remains unclear. RESEARCH QUESTION: Do eye closure and foam support alter anterior-posterior (AP) center-of-pressure (CoP) frequency composition, and are these changes associated with regional hemoglobin fluctuations and interregional coupling. METHODS: Forty-five healthy young adults completed eyes-open and eyes-closed standing on firm and foam surfaces. AP CoP relative energy was examined in four intervals: < 0.10, 0.10-0.50, 0.50-1.0, and 1.0-2.0 Hz. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) measured oxygenated hemoglobin (HbO) fluctuations and interregional coupling. Repeated-measures analyses of variance were supplemented by baseline-adjusted correlations and influence-sensitivity analyses. RESULTS: Eye closure and foam support increased relative energy in the 0.50-1.0 Hz interval. Prefrontal-sensorimotor and premotor-parietal HbO coupling decreased on foam. The left-parietal interaction did not survive correction across eight bilateral regions. Changes in CoP relative energy were positively associated with parietal HbO fluctuations and negatively associated with interregional coupling. Association directions were unchanged in rank-based, leave-one-participant-out, and demographic-adjusted analyses. SIGNIFICANCE: Sensory-challenged standing was accompanied by covariation between AP sway frequency composition and task-epoch HbO measures. The findings link postural output to hemodynamic responses without identifying the sensory weights underlying that output.

articles.title: Beyond the Hangover: Associations Between Binge Drinking, Health, and Performance in Young Adult Resistance-Trained Females.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Chester M Sokolowski, Hannah K Eberhardt, Hunter J Mitchell et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: The present study aimed to evaluate associations between resistance training and binge drinking in relation to musculoskeletal composition, physical fitness, cognitive function, and psychological wellness in young adult females. METHODS: Participants were categorized into four groups: sedentary low alcohol consumers (SL; n=12), sedentary binge drinkers (SB; n=12), resistance-trained low alcohol consumers (RTL; n=12), and resistance-trained binge drinkers (RTB; n=12). Measurements included body composition via DEXA scan, muscle quality via ultrasonography, and insulin sensitivity via oral glucose tolerance test. Physical performance was assessed using maximum chair stand power, vertical jump, broad jump, knee extensor torque, grip strength, and push-ups to failure. Tests and questionnaires were used to assess cognitive function and psychological wellness. RESULTS: Resistance-trained females had lower body fat than sedentary females (RTL = 29.28±4.27%; RTB = 29.03±3.67%; SL = 37.18±5.32%; SB = 34.83±3.54%; p<0.05), and RTL had more fat-free mass than SL and SB (RTL = 48.31±5.81 kg; SL = 38.08±6.59 kg; SB = 40.37±6.05 kg; both p<0.05). There were no differences between RTL and RTB in bone mineral density, muscle quality, or physical performance. RTL outperformed SL and SB on vertical jump (both p<0.05) while RTB outperformed SL and SB on broad jump. RTL had lower fasting blood glucose than RTB (88.92±12.09 mg/dL and 103.17 ± 10.21 mg/dL, respectively; p=0.008), and lower postprandial blood glucose than all groups (RTL = 103.83±19.82 mg/dL; RTB = 137.58±21.54 mg/dL; SL = 148.50±44.60 mg/dL; SB = 139.25±14.49 mg/dL; all p<0.05). CONCLUSIONS: The results suggest that ≥1 year of binge drinking is associated with poorer metabolic health without differences in performance in young females. Further, frequent RT may mitigate the effects of binge drinking on body composition.

articles.title: Examination of Performance Anxiety Theories in Sport Psychology Textbooks and a Proposed Framework for Organizing These Theories.
articles.authors: Steven R Wininger, Lindsey Wheeler, Antony D Norman
articles.abstract: What are the major theories of performance anxiety, and what key variable sets do they share? Although many sport psychologists utilize specific performance anxiety theories to guide client treatments, we doubt many are familiar with the full spectrum of available theories and their associated variables. This knowledge gap may lead to the selection of suboptimal treatment plans. We examined sport psychology textbooks to assess which theories are commonly presented, evaluated the accuracy of their presentation, and developed a categorization system based on common key variables. We analyzed 16 unique sport psychology textbooks, with independent coders reviewing each textbook. Twenty-five unique theories were identified, 10 of which appeared in five or more textbooks. We were surprised by the frequency of incomplete or inaccurate presentations of the theories and by the absence of a coherent framework for organizing these theories. We discuss applied implications for educators, practitioners, and textbook authors, introduce a proposed categorization system for organizing theories by key variables, and offer recommendations for future research.

articles.title: Heat acclimation does not alleviate the reduction in exogenous glucose oxidation that occurs when exercising in hot conditions.
articles.authors: Tim Podlogar, Rachel E Gifford, Joel Thomas et al.
articles.abstract: Exogenous glucose oxidation (CHOexo) is suppressed during endurance exercise performed in hot conditions, although the underlying mechanisms and effects of heat acclimation are unknown. The present study investigated whether heat acclimation alleviates the heat-induced suppression of CHOexo and the underlying physiological mechanisms. Seventeen endurance-trained adults (10 males and seven females) completed 90 min cycling trials at 45% Wmax with glucose ingestion (90 g·h-1) under temperate [20°C; 20% relative humidity (RH); COOL] and hot (40°C; 20% RH; HOT) conditions, and again in the heat (40°C; 20% RH; POST) following a heat acclimation protocol (9 days of isothermic exercise-heat acclimation across a 10 day period). Dual stable isotope tracers ([U13C6] glucose ingestion, [6,6-2H2]glucose-infusion), indirect calorimetry and muscle biopsies were used to assess CHOexo, glucose kinetics and muscle glycogen utilisation during exercise. CHOexo (mean [95% confidence limits]) was reduced by ∼27% in HOT compared to COOL (0.37 [0.31, 0.43] g·min-1 vs. 0.51 [0.45, 0.57] g·min-1; P < 0.001) and, despite clear thermoregulatory adaptation following heat acclimation, remained suppressed in POST (0.38 [0.31, 0.44] g·min-1; P < 0.01 vs. COOL). Rates of plasma glucose appearance, disappearance and exogenous glucose appearance were unaffected by environmental condition or heat acclimation. Glucose metabolic clearance rates and plasma glucose oxidation were reduced in HOT and POST compared to COOL (P < 0.05). A decreased capacity for plasma glucose disposal and utilisation rather than limitations in splanchnic glucose appearance underpin the reduced exogenous glucose oxidation observed during exercise in the heat, and this is not alleviated by heat acclimation. KEY POINTS: Exogenous glucose oxidation is suppressed during endurance-exercise performed in hot conditions, although the underlying mechanisms and effects of heat acclimation are unknown. A decreased capacity for plasma glucose disposal and utilisation rather than limitations in splanchnic glucose appearance appear to underpin the reduced exogenous glucose oxidation observed during exercise in the heat. Heat acclimation does not alleviate the reduction in exogenous glucose oxidation that occurs when exercising in hot conditions.

articles.title: Body composition and blood pressure: Haemodynamic links in young men and women.
articles.authors: Domonkos Cseh, Jessica E Middlemiss, Shikai Yu et al.
articles.abstract: The aim of this study was to explore the sex-specific haemodynamic links between body composition parameters and systolic and diastolic blood pressure (SBP and DBP, respectively) in adults free of cardiovascular disease and not receiving cardiovascular medications. Body mass index (BMI), fat mass (FM), fat-free mass (FFM), SBP and DBP, cardiac output (CO), peripheral vascular resistance (PVR) and aortic pulse wave velocity (PWV) were determined in 235 men and 192 women aged 18-40 years. Multivariable linear regression and single- as well as multiple-mediator models were used to assess haemodynamic mechanisms underlying the associations between body composition and blood pressure. BMI showed positive associations with SBP and DBP in both sexes (P < 0.001 for all). In men, FFM was the main body composition correlate of SBP (P < 0.001), with the positive association driven in part by CO and partially offset by opposing effects through PVR. FM was the dominant body composition correlate of DBP in men and both SBP and DBP in women (P < 0.001 for all), with the positive associations mediated by PVR and PWV in both sexes, and additionally by heart rate in the FM-DBP association in men. Changes in FFM may affect SBP predominantly through CO in young men. Changes in FM may affect DBP in young men and both SBP and DBP in young women, predominantly through vascular mechanisms. These findings provide important insights into sex differences in the physiology of adiposity-related BP changes in young adults and may help inform sex-specific strategies for the management of adiposity-related hypertension.

articles.title: Global Positioning System-Derived Match Demands and Their Association With On-Field Technical Performance in Elite Australian Football League Women's (AFLW) Athletes.
articles.journal: International journal of sports physiology and performance
articles.authors: Brooke Jenner, Hunter Bennett, Steven Milanese et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: This study sought to determine the associations between global positioning system-derived match demands and technical performance in elite Australian Football League Women's athletes. METHODS: Global positioning system match demands (total distance, speed, acceleration, high-intensity running [>19 km·h-1], very high-intensity running [>21 km·h-1], sprint distances [>24 km·h-1]) were measured with Catapult Vector S7 global positioning system units during the 2023 and 2024 seasons. Champion Data ranking points and best and fairest votes for each game were considered technical performance outcomes. Linear mixed effects regression models examined associations between match demands and technical performance, adjusting for season, ground location, and playing position. RESULTS: Five hundred sixty-six player match profiles from 32 athletes across the 2 seasons were analyzed. Ranking points were significantly (P < .001) associated with total distance (R2 = .29 [95% CI .22-.40]), speed (R2 = .01 [.00-.15]), and acceleration (R2 = .09 [.00-.23]). Best and fairest votes were significantly (P < .001) associated with total distance (R2 = .23 [.17-.34]), speed (R2 = .01 [.00-.11]), acceleration (R2 = .05 [.00-.17]), and very high-intensity running distance per minute (R2 = .00 [.00-.13]). CONCLUSIONS: Total distance, speed, acceleration, and very high-intensity running distance per minute were associated with Champion Data ranking points and best and fairest votes across Australian Football League Women's seasons 2023 and 2024. This suggests that athletes who cover greater total distances and achieve higher average acceleration get more opportunities to be involved in match-play and demonstrate higher levels of technical performance.

articles.title: VRCycle: A Feasibility Randomized Controlled Trial Evaluating a Virtual Reality Cycling Intervention in People With Knee Osteoarthritis.
articles.authors: Erin MacIntyre, Jaime Jordán-López, Daiki Kasai et al.
articles.abstract: IMPORTANCE: Exercise is recommended as a core treatment for knee osteoarthritis; yet uptake is suboptimal, with identified barriers including pain, difficulty (overly effortful), and boredom. Virtual reality (VR) shows promise in overcoming these barriers, although whether VR-enhanced exercise is acceptable to people with osteoarthritis and feasible in physical therapy settings is unknown. OBJECTIVE: The objective was to assess the feasibility of conducting a clinical trial to evaluate VR-enhanced cycling and explore preliminary efficacy of this intervention. DESIGN: A prospectively registered (ACTRN12624000122550), two-arm feasibility randomized controlled trial was conducted. SETTING: The trial was conducted at a clinical trials facility. PARTICIPANTS: Forty-one participants with painful knee osteoarthritis were enrolled. INTERVENTIONS: Participants were randomized (1:1 ratio) to receive VR-enhanced cycling or traditional (no-VR) cycling, both involving twelve, 30-minute cycling sessions over 6-weeks, supervised by a physical therapist. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: A priori feasibility criteria surrounding recruitment and enrolment rate, intervention adherence, technical difficulty, retention, and participant experience (acceptability, credibility, adverse events) were evaluated. Clinical outcomes (pain, function) and exercise capacity (perceptually regulated exercise test) were assessed at baseline, post-intervention, 1-month follow-up (clinical outcomes only). Within-session exercise engagement (work, time) and experience (perceived exertion, affect) were evaluated as process variables. RESULTS: All feasibility criteria were met. An average of 6.8 participants per week were eligible with a 73% enrollment rate. Participants attended 91% of intervention sessions, and 90% of participants completed follow-up assessments. VR technical issues were rare (3% of sessions) as were adverse events (2 unrelated to VR). Treatment acceptability and credibility was high and clinical outcomes improved in both groups. CONCLUSIONS: Progression to a full trial is supported due to high feasibility, acceptability, and improvement in clinical outcomes. RELEVANCE: Although not powered to evaluate efficacy, the within-group changes observed demonstrate that both cycling modalities can improve knee pain, function, and exercise capacity.

articles.title: Cross-sectional Associations of Ultra-processed Food Intake with Cardiometabolic Risk Differ by Nutritional Quality.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Tonja R Nansel, Amara Channell Doig, Neil Perkins et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Ambiguity regarding whether the health effects of ultra-processed food intake are attributable to nutritional quality and/or industrial processing hinders effective food policies and dietary guidelines. OBJECTIVE: This study examined how cross-sectional associations of ultra-processed food intake with cardiometabolic risk factors differ by nutritional quality. METHODS: This cross-sectional study used data from adults age 20+ years with two 24-hour dietary recalls in the 2017-2020 U.S. National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (n=6525). Reported foods were classified as moderation or non-moderation using validated criteria for added sugar, sodium, refined grains, carbohydrate-to-fiber ratio, saturated and total fat, and alcohol. Percent of energy intake from moderation and non-moderation foods was calculated for each Nova food processing classification. Linear regression models estimated associations of moderation and non-moderation Nova subtype intakes with body mass index (BMI), waist circumference, percent body fat, blood lipids (total cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, triglycerides), glycohemoglobin, fasting glucose and insulin, C-reactive protein (CRP), and blood pressure. RESULTS: Moderation and non-moderation ultra-processed food comprised (mean±SE) 48±0.7% and 6±0.2% of energy intake, respectively. Coefficient estimates (representing the difference associated with replacing 1% of energy intake from Nova 1-3 foods) for positive associations of moderation ultra-processed food intake with BMI (β; 95% CI 0.03; 0.02, 0.05), waist circumference (cm) (0.08; 0.05, 0.1), percent body fat (0.05; 0.02, 0.09), insulin (μU/mL) (0.07; 0.04, 0.1), and CRP (mg/L) (0.01; 0.007, 0.02) were different from the null associations of non-moderation ultra-processed food intake (p=0.006, p=0.01, p=0.01, p<0.001, p=0.003, respectively). In models including all Nova subtypes, moderation minimally processed food intake was associated with higher adiposity indicators and glucose, relative to non-moderation minimally processed food intake. CONCLUSIONS: Associations of ultra-processed and minimally processed food intakes with multiple cardiometabolic risk factors differ based on nutritional quality classification, supporting policies and guidelines targeting nutritional quality.

articles.title: Folate and folic acid intake in relation to molecular subtypes of colorectal cancer: pooled analyses of up to 8970 cases and 8098 control participants.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Bethany Van Guelpen, Björn Gylling, Sophia Harlid et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Higher intakes of the B-vitamin folate are associated with modest reductions in colorectal cancer risk. Intertumoral heterogeneity has been suggested to affect the relationship, but studies to date have been limited in number and size. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to determine whether associations between intake of the B-vitamin folate (from diet and folic acid supplements) and the risk of colorectal cancer vary by tumor molecular marker status for BRAF and KRAS mutations, microsatellite instability (MSI), and/or the CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP). METHODS: The full study population included 8970 colorectal cancer cases and 8098 control participants from observational case-control and cohort studies within the Genetics and Epidemiology of Colorectal Cancer Consortium (GECCO) and the Colon Cancer Family Registry (CCFR). Folate intake was assessed by food frequency questionnaire or diet history. Multivariable odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using multinomial logistic regression. Differences in associations between tumor subtypes were assessed using case-only logistic regression. RESULTS: Total folate intake and folate supplement use were inversely associated with the risk of colorectal cancer, whereas the relationship for dietary folate was weaker. These associations did not vary substantially among CRC subtypes defined by individual tumor markers. Possible heterogeneity was observed only for CIMP, with a stronger inverse association between total folate intake and CIMP-low/negative compared to CIMP-high colorectal cancer (pdifference=0.07). Associations were also inverse for total folate and subtypes defined by marker combinations, except for a null association for the less common Jass Type 2 subtype of MSS/MSI-low, CIMP-high, BRAF-mutated, KRAS-wildtype (pdifference=0.06 compared to the traditional adenoma-carcinoma pathway). CONCLUSIONS: Overall, the putative protective effect of folate intake in colorectal cancer development appears to be broad, not limited to specific subtypes defined by BRAF, KRAS, MSI, and CIMP status, or combinations of these markers, in the tumor.

articles.title: Total energy expenditure of elite female cheerleaders assessed by doubly labeled water.
articles.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
articles.authors: Mamiko Ichikawa, Yoichi Hatamoto, Aya Itoi et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: This study aimed to quantify total energy expenditure (TEE) and physical activity level (PAL) in elite female competitive cheerleaders during the in-season period using the doubly labeled water (DLW) method. METHODS: Fifteen Division 1 collegiate female competitive cheerleaders in Japan were included in the analysis. TEE was measured over seven consecutive days under free-living conditions using the DLW method. Body mass (BM) and body composition were assessed using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry. PAL was calculated as the ratio of TEE to resting metabolic rate estimated from fat-free mass. RESULTS: Mean TEE was 2,591 ± 440 kcal·d-1 (range: 1,748-3,264 kcal·d-1), and mean PAL was 2.21 ± 0.17 (range: 1.97-2.52). TEE showed strong positive correlations with BM (r = 0.993, p < 0.001) and fat-free mass (r = 0.995, p < 0.001). No significant change in BM was observed over the measurement period. CONCLUSIONS: This study provides the first direct assessment of TEE in elite female cheerleaders using the DLW method. The high TEE and PAL observed during the in-season period indicate that competitive cheerleading imposes substantial energetic demands comparable to those of other high-intensity sports. These findings contribute essential reference data for understanding the energy expenditure characteristics of competitive cheerleaders and may support the development of evidence-based training and health management strategies for this population.
